question: Two capacitors connected across the same two nodes are said to be in...
explanation: Parts connected across the same two nodes are in parallel and share the same voltage.

Why do capacitors in series all carry the same charge?
options: Because they all have the same capacitance
Because the voltage across each is the same
Because the source divides charge equally
Because each middle node is an isolated island that must stay neutral, so whatever charge appears on one side appears with opposite sign on the other
explanation: Nothing can flow onto or off a node that only touches capacitor plates. It starts neutral and stays neutral, which forces equal charge Q on every capacitor in the chain.

question: What is 4.7 uF in series with 10 uF?
explanation: C = (4.7 x 10) / (4.7 + 10) = 47 / 14.7 = 3.197 uF, smaller than the smaller capacitor.

question: 1 uF and 2 uF are in series across 9 V. Which one has more voltage across it?
explanation: Both carry Q = (2/3 uF) x 9 V = 6 uC. V = Q / C gives 6 V on the 1 uF and 3 V on the 2 uF: the smaller capacitor gets the larger share.

question: A 6.3 V capacitor and a 25 V capacitor are connected in parallel. What is the safe working voltage of the pair?
explanation: In parallel both see the same voltage, so the lowest rating limits the pair: 6.3 V.

question: Why do series capacitor banks often have a resistor across each capacitor?
options: To force an even DC voltage split despite unequal leakage currents
To make the bank charge faster
To turn the capacitors into resistors at high frequency
explanation: Over long times leakage decides how voltage is shared, and leakage varies a lot between parts. Balancing resistors carry more current than the leakage and set an even split.
